followUps:
Keep bash for short glue: an entrypoint that sets environment variables and runs one command, a one-screen wrapper around tar, rsync or systemctl, and anything that is mostly pipes between existing tools.

Bash is everywhere with no install step, so it suits container entrypoints, CI steps and boot hooks. Rule of thumb: if the script is under about 20 lines, has no real data handling and fails fine with set -euo pipefail, leave it. A Python tool can still call these wrappers.

Pass the command as a list, never as one string, and always set a timeout and check the result.

r = subprocess.run(["./backup.sh", path],
    capture_output=True, text=True,
    timeout=300, check=True)
print(r.stdout)

A list avoids the shell, so a path like a; rm -rf / is just one odd argument. check=True raises CalledProcessError on a non-zero exit, and timeout raises TimeoutExpired so a hung script cannot block the job forever. Avoid shell=True with user data.

The instance role wins. Explicit environment variables are checked before the instance profile, so AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID beats the role.

boto3 walks a fixed chain: explicit arguments to the client or session, then environment variables, then the shared credentials and config files (profiles, SSO), then container credentials, and last the EC2 instance metadata role. So a stale key left in the environment silently overrides the role, and calls may run as the wrong identity. That is why the script prints sts.get_caller_identity() first and compares the account id.

IMDSv2 needs a session token, which blocks the simple request forgery attacks that steal role credentials through IMDSv1.

With IMDSv1 any plain GET to 169.254.169.254 returns the role keys, so a server-side request forgery bug in an app ("fetch this URL") can leak them. IMDSv2 first needs a PUT request to get a token and the token must be sent in a header; forwarded requests usually cannot do that. You enforce it with HttpTokens=required, and a small hop limit of 1 stops containers from reaching it. boto3 uses IMDSv2 automatically.

code.title: Pagination: one call misses pages
code.python:
# Pagination: one call sees only the first page; a loop follows the token.
KEYS = ["key-%04d" % i for i in range(2500)]   # pretend bucket with 2500 objects
PAGE = 1000

def list_page(token=None):
    start = int(token) if token else 0
    chunk = KEYS[start:start + PAGE]
    nxt = str(start + PAGE) if start + PAGE < len(KEYS) else None
    return {"Keys": chunk, "NextToken": nxt}

def list_all():
    token, seen = None, set()
    while True:
        resp = list_page(token)
        yield from resp["Keys"]
        token = resp["NextToken"]
        if token is None:          # only stop when there is no token
            return
        if token in seen:          # guard against a stuck token
            raise RuntimeError("repeated token")
        seen.add(token)

print("bucket really holds:", len(KEYS))
print("single call sees   :", len(list_page()["Keys"]), "(bug: silently partial)")
print("paginated loop sees:", sum(1 for _ in list_all()))
# Time O(N) over N keys, space O(page) because it is a generator.

followUps:
Stop the loop as soon as you find the item; a paginator or generator only fetches the next page when you ask for it.

for page in paginator.paginate(Bucket=b):
    for o in page.get("Contents", []):
        if o["Key"] == target:
            return o
# or: paginate(PaginationConfig={"MaxItems": 50})

With 1000 keys per page, finding an object on page 2 costs 2 calls, not the whole 2500-key listing. Remember Contents is missing on empty pages.

Narrow the listing on the server side, or do not list at all: use a Prefix, keep an index, or use S3 Inventory.

Listing 1 billion keys at 1000 per call is 1 million requests, which is slow and costs money. Better options: a key layout with date prefixes so you list only today's prefix; S3 Inventory, which writes a daily CSV or Parquet report you can process in bulk; S3 Lifecycle rules, which expire objects without any script; and event notifications that record keys as they are created.

Catching Exception around the whole loop hides real problems and also stops the run on the first bad item.

It would treat a harmless NotFound the same as AccessDenied, and it catches typos like a KeyError from your own bug, then reports success. Catch ClientError narrowly inside the loop, around one item, decide skip, stop or fail, and count failures. Use a broad catch only at the very top to log the crash and exit non-zero. Example: 1000 items with 3 locked ones should delete 997, report 3, and exit 1.

DryRunOperation is the error EC2 returns when you pass DryRun=True and you do have permission, so the call would have worked.

EC2 never performs the action in this mode. If permission is missing you get UnauthorizedOperation instead. So the check is: catch ClientError, and if the code is DryRunOperation treat it as "allowed"; any other code is a real problem. It is a cheap way to test IAM permissions before the real run. Not every AWS service supports DryRun, mainly EC2 does.

code.title: Backoff with full jitter and retry rules
code.python:
import random

BASE, CAP, MAX_TRIES = 1.0, 30.0, 6

def full_jitter(attempt, rng):
    # wait = uniform(0, min(cap, base * 2**attempt))
    return rng.uniform(0, min(CAP, BASE * 2 ** attempt))

def should_retry(status):
    # retry throttling and server errors; never retry other 4xx
    return status in (408, 429) or 500 <= status <= 599

print("upper bound per retry:", [min(CAP, BASE * 2 ** a) for a in range(5)])
print("worst case total (5 retries):", sum(min(CAP, BASE * 2 ** a) for a in range(5)), "s")
for s in (200, 400, 403, 404, 429, 500, 503):
    print(s, "retry" if should_retry(s) else "no retry")

rng = random.Random(7)
responses = iter([503, 429, 503, 200])      # fake flaky server
for attempt in range(MAX_TRIES):
    status = next(responses)
    if status == 200:
        print("attempt", attempt + 1, "-> success")
        break
    if not should_retry(status):
        print("fatal", status); break
    wait = full_jitter(attempt, rng)        # a real script would time.sleep(wait)
    print("attempt", attempt + 1, "->", status, "wait %.2fs" % wait)
# Bounded: at most MAX_TRIES calls, so the job fails visibly instead of hanging.

followUps:
The worst case is 31 seconds in total for 5 retries, because the delays are capped at 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds.

With full jitter each wait is a random number between 0 and min(30, 1*2^n), so the upper bounds are 1+2+4+8+16 = 31 s. The cap of 30 only starts to matter at the 6th retry (32 would become 30). On average the total is about half, near 15.5 s. Without jitter the waits are exactly 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and every client retries at the same moment.

It retries only methods in an allowed list, by default the idempotent ones, and only for status codes you list.

Retry(total=5, backoff_factor=1,
      status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504],
      allowed_methods=["GET", "HEAD", "PUT", "DELETE"])

By default POST is excluded because a repeat could create two orders. Connection errors before the request is sent are safe to retry for any method. Add POST only when the API accepts an idempotency key. respect_retry_after_header is on by default.

code.title: Safe snapshot cleanup plan, dry run first
code.python:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

NOW = datetime(2026, 11, 15, tzinfo=timezone.utc)   # fixed so the output is stable
DAYS = 30
snaps = [
    {"Id": "snap-1", "Tags": [], "StartTime": NOW - timedelta(days=45)},
    {"Id": "snap-2", "Tags": [{"Key": "Owner", "Value": "x"}], "StartTime": NOW - timedelta(days=90)},
    {"Id": "snap-3", "Tags": [], "StartTime": NOW - timedelta(days=10)},
    {"Id": "snap-4", "Tags": [], "StartTime": NOW - timedelta(days=30)},        # boundary
    {"Id": "snap-5", "Tags": [], "StartTime": NOW - timedelta(days=30, seconds=1)},
]

def plan(snapshots, now, days, max_count=3):
    cutoff = now - timedelta(days=days)           # pure function: no AWS calls
    todo = [s["Id"] for s in snapshots if not s["Tags"] and s["StartTime"] < cutoff]
    if len(todo) > max_count:                     # circuit breaker
        raise SystemExit("plan too large: %d" % len(todo))
    return todo

def run(apply):
    todo = plan(snaps, NOW, DAYS)
    for sid in todo:
        print(("DELETE " if apply else "would delete ") + sid)
    print("total:", len(todo), "(dry run)" if not apply else "(applied)")

print("input ids:", [s["Id"] for s in snaps])
run(apply=False)      # dry run is the default

followUps:
Add a manifest of already-managed resources: query Backup tags and exclude whatever AWS Backup owns.

Backup-created snapshots carry tags such as aws:backup:source-resource, and they are named like awsbackup:job-..., but those tags may not be visible in all cases, so also ask AWS Backup for its recovery points. Safest rule: only delete when you can prove the snapshot is yours. Same for Data Lifecycle Manager (aws:dlm:lifecycle-policy-id tag). Skip anything referenced by an AMI (the delete fails with InvalidSnapshot.InUse) and report the skipped ones.

Loop over the accounts, assume a read/write role in each one, and run the same code per region, with a cap per account.

for acct in org.list_accounts():
    creds = sts.assume_role(RoleArn=arn(acct),
                RoleSessionName="cleanup")
    for region in regions:
        run(session(creds, region), acct)

List accounts with organizations.list_accounts (paginated). Keep the account guard per session, write one plan file per account, roll out dry-run first, and run accounts in parallel with a small worker pool (say 5) to avoid throttling. One failing account should not stop the others.

code.title: Idempotent reconciler: second run changes nothing

followUps:
"Check then create" is not enough when two runs can happen at the same time, because both can check, see nothing, and both create.

Example: two jobs both look for volume "data-1", find none, and both create it, so you pay for two. The gap between check and create is a race. Fix it by making the create itself atomic: a ClientToken, a DynamoDB ConditionExpression=attribute_not_exists(pk), an S3 conditional write, or a unique name that the service rejects with "already exists" (then treat that error as success).

Use a lease: a lock record in a shared store that one host holds for a limited time.

DynamoDB works well: PutItem with ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(pk) OR expires_at < :now". Whoever succeeds owns it and renews while working. A lock file on NFS is unreliable, and flock is per machine only. Other options are etcd or Consul sessions, a database advisory lock, or simply running the job in exactly one place.

A bare Mock accepts any call, so a typo or a wrong parameter still passes while real AWS would reject it.

Stubber wraps a real boto3 client and checks every expected call against the real API model: wrong parameter names or types raise an error, and assert_no_pending_responses() fails if a call you expected never happened. create_autospec gives a similar guard for your own classes. Example: Mock().delete_snapshot(SnapshotID="x") passes, but the real parameter is SnapshotId.

moto does not check IAM permissions or real service limits, so a test can pass while the real run gets AccessDenied.

By default moto accepts any call from any fake identity. It also does not fully reproduce throttling, eventual consistency, or every error code and edge case of each service, and some newer features are missing. So keep a short sandbox-account run before release, using the real role. Mocks prove your logic; only AWS proves permissions and limits.

Duplicate keys are silently accepted by the standard parsers (the last one wins), so you must detect them yourself while parsing.

For JSON use object_pairs_hook, which receives the key/value pairs before they become a dict.

def no_dups(pairs):
    keys = [k for k, _ in pairs]
    if len(keys) != len(set(keys)):
        raise ValueError("duplicate key")
    return dict(pairs)
json.loads(text, object_pairs_hook=no_dups)

For YAML, yamllint has a key-duplicates rule, and ruamel.yaml raises DuplicateKeyError by default.

Stream it instead of loading it: a 5 GB file would need many gigabytes of memory as Python objects.

If it is a JSON Lines file (one object per line) just iterate over the lines, memory stays tiny. For one huge JSON array use an incremental parser such as ijson (a third-party package) that yields items one at a time. Or pre-filter with jq -c '.items[]' into lines. Process in batches and write results out as you go, so memory is O(one item) and time is O(N).

Use preventive controls as the source of truth and let Terraform own the values, with the tool only touching resources Terraform does not manage.

Set required tags in Terraform with default_tags on the provider. The tool should skip resources that carry a Terraform marker tag, or only report them as drift. If it must tag them, tell Terraform to ignore those keys with ignore_changes = [tags["Owner"]]. Otherwise Terraform sets Owner=A, the tool sets Owner=B, and the two loop forever at every run.

Roll out in stages: report only, then one test account, then small groups, with the cap and an easy stop.

  1. Week 1: dry run in all 40 accounts, share the reports.
  2. Apply in 1 sandbox account.
  3. Apply to 5 accounts, then 15, then all 40.

Use a per-account flag in a config file in Git, a per-run change cap (say 200 tags), and alerts when failures appear. Tagging is easily reversible, which makes it a safe first apply mode.

code.title: Non-blocking lock stops overlapping runs
code.python:
import fcntl, os, tempfile

path = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "demo-job.lock")

def try_lock():
    fd = open(path, "w")
    try:
        fcntl.flock(fd, fcntl.LOCK_EX | fcntl.LOCK_NB)   # non-blocking
        return fd
    except BlockingIOError:
        fd.close()
        return None

first = try_lock()
print("run A got lock:", first is not None)
second = try_lock()          # simulates the next cron run starting too early
print("run B got lock:", second is not None)
if second is None:
    print("run B: already running, exiting 0")
first.close()                # releasing (or process exit) frees the lock
third = try_lock()
print("run C got lock after A finished:", third is not None)
if third:
    third.close()
os.remove(path)

followUps:
Watch for it by recording every run, including the ones that exit early, and alerting when too many were skipped in a row.

When the lock is busy the job logs "already running" and emits a metric skipped_runs. Also write a last_success timestamp and alert if it is older than, say, 2 hours for an hourly job (a dead-man's switch such as a heartbeat check). One skip is normal; 3 skips in a row means the job now takes longer than its schedule, so fix the speed or the interval.

A lease is a lock that is granted for a fixed time, so it frees itself if the holder dies.

Without an expiry, a host that crashes or loses the network while holding the lock blocks everyone forever. With a 10-minute lease, others can take over after it runs out. The holder should renew every minute or so while it works. Careful: a slow holder may still be working after expiry, so writes should carry a fencing token (an increasing number) that the storage checks, rejecting the older holder.

Use a pinned lockfile and install from one trusted index, so every server gets the same versions.

Build a wheel in CI on each tag, then install with pipx install tool==1.4.2 or uv tool install using a constraints or lock file (pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt). Pin transitive dependencies too: if requests is unpinned, servers installed a month apart can differ. For full control ship a container image, which freezes Python itself and the OS libraries.

CGO_ENABLED=0 makes Go build a fully static binary that does not use the C library, so it runs on any Linux machine or in an empty container.

With cgo on, the binary may link to glibc, and then it can break on Alpine (musl) or on an older distribution. With it off, the standard library uses pure Go code (for example for DNS). Typical build: CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build. You lose packages that need C, such as some SQLite drivers.

Check generated code against a fixed checklist of the usual dangerous gaps, then run it through the same tests as any other code.

  • Uses a paginator, and has a test with 2 or more pages?
  • Timeouts and one retry layer only?
  • Dry run default, account guard, change cap?
  • ClientError handled by code, not a blanket except?
  • No shell=True, no yaml.load, UTC-aware datetimes?
  • No hardcoded keys; real API names (models invent parameters)?

Give the agent a narrow tool with a read-only plan step and make the apply step need a human approval.

Expose two functions: plan_cleanup(account, days) returns the list and a plan id; apply_cleanup(plan_id) only runs for a plan a person approved, within a change cap. The agent's role has read-only permissions, the apply role is assumed by the tool itself, never by the agent. Every call is logged. It cannot pass arbitrary IDs, so a confused agent cannot delete anything outside the plan.
